## Defaults that go wrong

Every fix in this page has a default, and every default is occasionally a disaster.
Dropping incomplete rows is the R default and it can quietly delete a season. Replacing
missing values with the mean is the commonest imputation and it manufactures data that
was never observed. Removing outliers is standard practice and it is how genuine
extreme events get erased from the record.

None of these decisions is technical. Each one requires you to know why the value is
missing, or why the number is strange.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs.qmd >}}

## The idea

### Three kinds of missing

The distinction matters because only one of them is harmless.

**Missing completely at random.** The chance of a value being absent has nothing to do
with anything; a technician dropped a tube. Rare in practice. Dropping these rows costs
you precision and nothing else.

**Missing at random** (a badly named category). The chance depends on things you *did*
observe: chlorophyll is missing more often in winter, and you recorded the season.
Dropping the rows biases your sample; imputation using the observed variables can
repair much of it.

**Missing not at random.** The chance depends on the missing value itself. A sensor
that fails in rough weather, and rough weather is when the interesting mixing happens.
A net that fails to retain the smallest individuals. Nothing in the data can fix this,
and no imputation method will tell you that you have it. You have to know your
instrument.

Our chlorophyll gap is the middle case: 19% missing in winter, 1% in autumn, with
season recorded. But ask *why* the winter values are absent. If it is cloud cover
blocking an ocean-colour sensor, then cloudy days are missing, and cloud affects
light, which affects chlorophyll. Framed that way, the same gap is closer to the third
kind.

### Outliers come in three kinds too

**Impossible values.** A depth of 1581 m on a 200 m shelf. A salinity of $-999$. These
are errors. Correct them if you can reconstruct the truth, otherwise mark them missing.

**Genuine extremes.** A single haul with 400 individuals during a spawning aggregation.
This is the most valuable observation in your dataset, and "outlier removal" deletes it.
Extreme is not the same as wrong.

**Plausible errors.** The two depths that are ten times too deep but land inside the
normal range. Undetectable, and they stay in your data.

::: {.callout-warning}
"More than three standard deviations from the mean" is not a definition of an error. It
is a definition of rare, and in ecological count data rare values are usually the real
ones. Remove a value because you can say what is wrong with it, not because it is far
from the middle.
:::

### Measurement error

The vessel offset found on the [previous page](exploratory-analysis.qmd) is not a
missing value or an outlier. It is a systematic bias in an instrument, and it affects
every row that vessel collected. Three options, in descending order of preference:
correct it against a calibration standard; include `vessel` as a feature so the model
can absorb the offset; or drop salinity, which here costs nothing since salinity has no
real effect.

### Class imbalance

When one class is rare, as with the 5% rare species, two things follow. Accuracy becomes
meaningless, as [section 7 shows](../07-validation/classification-metrics.qmd). And the
fitting procedure itself is pulled towards the common class, because getting the
common class right is where the easy gains are.

Remedies exist: down-sampling the common class, up-sampling the rare one, synthetic
methods such as SMOTE, or class weights. All are available through the `themis` package
as recipe steps, and all come with the same condition:

::: {.callout-important}
Resampling for imbalance is applied to the **training data only**, never to the data you
evaluate on. Balancing your test set means measuring performance on a population that
does not exist. In `recipes` this is handled for you, since `themis` steps are skipped when
the recipe is applied to new data, but only if you use them inside a recipe rather than
balancing the table by hand beforehand.
:::

## Worked example

### Sentinels first

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: sentinels
clean <- raw |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(
    salinity_psu  = na_if(salinity_psu, -999),
    temperature_c = na_if(temperature_c, -999)
  )

clean |>
  summarise(across(c(temperature_c, salinity_psu, chlorophyll_mg_m3),
                   list(missing = \(x) sum(is.na(x)),
                        mean = \(x) round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 2))))
```

## Python

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_raw

raw = load_coastal_survey_raw()

clean = raw.drop_duplicates().copy()
clean["salinity_psu"] = clean["salinity_psu"].replace(-999, np.nan)
clean["temperature_c"] = clean["temperature_c"].replace(-999, np.nan)

columns = ["temperature_c", "salinity_psu", "chlorophyll_mg_m3"]
pd.DataFrame({
    "missing": clean[columns].isna().sum(),
    "mean": clean[columns].mean().round(2),   # pandas skips NaN, as na.rm does
})
```

:::

Salinity's mean moves from 2.24 to 33.9. Nothing was fixed in the data, and the `-999`s
are still missing values, but they are now *honestly* missing, and every summary
downstream stops lying.

### Categories

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: categories
clean <- clean |>
  mutate(substrate = str_to_lower(str_trim(substrate)),
         substrate = fct_collapse(substrate,
           sand   = c("sand", "sandy"),
           mud    = c("mud", "muddy"),
           gravel = "gravel",
           rock   = c("rock", "rocky")))

count(clean, substrate)
```

## Python

```python
substrate = clean["substrate"].str.strip().str.lower()
clean["substrate"] = substrate.replace(
    {"sandy": "sand", "muddy": "mud", "rocky": "rock"}
)

clean["substrate"].value_counts().reset_index()
```

:::

Note the judgement hidden in that block. Is `sandy` the same category as `sand`, or was
one observer distinguishing "sand" from "sandy mud"? We have merged them. On a real
survey this is a question for whoever recorded it, and the honest version of this code
comes with an answer, not an assumption.

### Impossible depths

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: depths
clean |> filter(depth_m > 250) |> select(station_id, depth_m) |> arrange(desc(depth_m))
```

## Python

```python
(clean.loc[clean["depth_m"] > 250, ["station_id", "depth_m"]]
    .sort_values("depth_m", ascending=False))
```

:::

Ten stations, all suspiciously close to ten times a plausible shelf depth. Dividing by
ten puts each one back into the range where its temperature makes sense, which is
evidence rather than convenience: a station recorded at 1392 m with 6 °C water is
impossible on this shelf, while the same station at 139 m is ordinary.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fix-depths
clean <- clean |> mutate(depth_m = if_else(depth_m > 250, depth_m / 10, depth_m))

range(clean$depth_m)
```

## Python

```python
clean["depth_m"] = clean["depth_m"].where(
    clean["depth_m"] <= 250, clean["depth_m"] / 10
)

(clean["depth_m"].min(), clean["depth_m"].max())
```

:::

Two of the twelve decimal errors are still in there, at 125 m and 166 m, and no
inspection will find them. That is the normal state of a cleaned dataset.

### The cost of complete-case deletion

The default in most modelling functions is to silently drop any row with a missing
value. Here is the bill.

```{r}
#| label: fig-deletion
#| fig-cap: "Season composition of the survey before and after dropping every row with a missing value. Winter loses about a fifth of its stations, and the dataset quietly becomes less wintry than the survey that produced it."
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart comparing the number of stations per season before and after complete-case deletion. Autumn, spring and summer barely change, while winter drops visibly from about 200 stations to about 160."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4
comparison <- bind_rows(
  clean |> count(season) |> mutate(dataset = "All rows"),
  clean |> drop_na() |> count(season) |> mutate(dataset = "Complete cases only")
)

ggplot(comparison, aes(season, n, fill = dataset)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.68) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Stations", fill = NULL,
       title = "Where the deleted rows come from")
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: deletion-cost
tibble(
  rows_before = nrow(clean),
  rows_after  = nrow(drop_na(clean)),
  lost        = nrow(clean) - nrow(drop_na(clean)),
  winter_lost_pct = round(100 * (1 - sum(drop_na(clean)$season == "winter") /
                                     sum(clean$season == "winter")), 1)
)
```

## Python

```python
complete = clean.dropna()
winter = clean["season"] == "winter"

pd.DataFrame({
    "rows_before": [len(clean)],
    "rows_after": [len(complete)],
    "lost": [len(clean) - len(complete)],
    "winter_lost_pct": [round(
        100 * (1 - (complete["season"] == "winter").sum() / winter.sum()), 1)],
})
```

:::

About 10% of rows overall, and a fifth of winter. If your question involves
winter conditions, the default has just removed a fifth of your evidence about them,
without a warning.

## Imputation as the alternative

The alternative is imputation: predict the missing chlorophyll values from the
variables you do have. `recipes` offers several steps:
`step_impute_median()`, `step_impute_knn()` and `step_impute_bag()`. The
[next page](scaling-and-encoding.qmd) puts them into a recipe properly.

Two conditions on imputation, both routinely broken:

**It must happen inside the resampling, not before.** Imputing with the median of the
whole dataset uses test-set values to fill training-set gaps. That is leakage, it is
easy to do by accident, and it is [the last page of this section](information-leakage.qmd).

**An imputed value is not an observation.** It is a prediction with uncertainty, and
treating it as data understates how little you know. Adding a `was_missing` indicator
column costs one feature and lets the model, and you, see where the gaps were.

For this dataset, the defensible chain is: sentinels to `NA`; categories standardised;
impossible depths corrected with a stated justification; chlorophyll imputed inside the
resampling with a missingness indicator; the vessel offset either corrected or absorbed
by including `vessel` as a feature. Not one of those steps is a default.

## Limits of these repairs

**Imputation cannot recover information that was never there.** With 19% of winter
chlorophyll missing, winter estimates will be weaker than summer ones whatever you do.
The honest response is to say so, not to impute until the table looks full.

**Correcting outliers can manufacture the pattern you are looking for.** We divided ten
depths by ten because the result fitted the rest of the survey. That reasoning is sound
and it is also how confirmation bias operates. State the rule, apply it uniformly, and
report how many rows it touched.

**Balancing classes changes what the model is estimating.** Down-sampling gives a model
trained on a 50/50 world when yours is 5/95, so its predicted probabilities no longer
mean what they say. [Section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) covers calibration.

**Cleaning is a scientific record, not a chore.** Every decision here changes the
results and should appear in the methods. "Data were cleaned in R" is not a method.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- Ask *why* a value is missing. Missing-in-winter and missing-at-random need different
  responses, and missing-because-of-the-value cannot be fixed at all.
- Complete-case deletion is the silent default. Here it removes about a fifth of
  winter.
- Impossible, extreme and plausible-but-wrong are three different kinds of outlier.
  Only the first is safely removed; the second is often your most valuable data.
- Systematic instrument bias is not an outlier. Correct it, or let the model see which
  instrument took each reading.
- Balance classes on the training data only, and expect predicted probabilities to shift
  when you do.
- Impute inside the resampling, never before it, and keep a record of where the gaps
  were.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Compare `step_impute_median()` with `step_impute_knn()` on chlorophyll. How different
   are the imputed winter values, and which set looks more like real winter chlorophyll?
2. Suppose the missing chlorophyll is caused by cloud, and cloud reduces light and hence
   chlorophyll. Which of the three kinds of missingness is that, and does any imputation
   method fix it?
